items.title: WriteBatch cost shift rationale
items.statement: Shifting WriteBatch construction to commit-time reduces in-memory retention and may improve throughput for high-replacement keys.
items.quote: Instead of holding this WriteBatch in-memory for the lifetime of the transaction, we can simply construct it during commit, by iterating the TreeMap and adding its contents to the WriteBatch.

items.rationale: To prevent OOM issues by halting processing until memory pressure is relieved via commit.
items.title: Pause processing on memory limit
items.statement: The StreamThread should halt processing once statestore.uncommitted.max.bytes is reached until the next commit succeeds.
items.quote: A more brute-force, but much simpler, approach would be for the StreamThread to halt processing once the statestore.uncommitted.max.bytes limit has been reached and not continue until the next commit succeeds.

items.rationale: To prevent OOM issues by waiting for a successful commit before continuing processing.
items.title: Pause processing on TimeoutException
items.statement: Processing should pause during a TimeoutException in commit and resume only after a successful commit.
items.quote: pausing processing under this circumstance could also be extended to a TimeoutException during commit: we would then wait for a successful commit before continuing processing, to prevent OOM issues.

items.title: Preferred solution combination
items.statement: The team leans towards combining pausing processing and deferring WriteBatch construction to commit-time.
items.quote: I'm starting to lean towards both fixes: pausing processing until the next successful commit and deferring the WriteBatch to commit-time.

items.title: Broker-side non-GSSAPI SASL triggers reverse DNS

items.title: Built-in non-GSSAPI mechanisms don't use serverName

items.rationale: The fix avoids reverse DNS for built-in non-GSSAPI mechanisms while preserving existing behavior for GSSAPI, custom mechanisms, and client-side SASL.

items.rationale: The serializer currently forces a deep copy from off-heap memory to return a byte array, which is inefficient for applications using custom off-heap pools.
items.title: Serializer forces deep copy for off-heap data
items.statement: The current serializer implementation requires a deep copy from custom off-heap pools to return a byte array.
items.quote: The serializer, currently, forces us to do a deep copy from our custom off-heap pool in order to return a "byte[]"...

items.rationale: Supporting ByteBuffer as a value type would allow users to manage pooled/reused buffers more efficiently, as the data is copied to the accumulator after serialization.
items.title: ByteBuffer support rationale
items.statement: Explicit support for ByteBuffer as a value type enables users to allocate and release buffers efficiently since data is copied to the accumulator after serialization.
items.quote: There appears to be more sense in explicit support for ByteBuffer as a value so that user code can allocate it before calling producer.send and release after that since it's guaranteed that the contents have been copied to producer's accumulator by then

items.rationale: To avoid errors, the value.serializer property must either be optional or ignored if the value is a ByteBuffer.
items.title: Handle value.serializer for ByteBuffer
items.statement: The value.serializer property must be made optional or ignored if the value is a ByteBuffer to prevent errors during producer construction or send invocation.
items.quote: If you make the value.serializer property optional, then there's a possibility of an error on the first send() invocation if the value happens to be anything other than ByteBuffer

items.rationale: A pull request was created to address the ByteBuffer support feature.
items.title: Pull request for ByteBuffer support
items.statement: A pull request (https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/10590) was created to implement ByteBuffer support.
items.quote: please see https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/10590

items.title: Sender thread behavior on auth failure
items.statement: The sender thread does not stop when KafkaProducer authentication fails.
items.quote: We don't stop the sender thread if authentication fails.

items.title: Purpose of auth failure exception
items.statement: An exception is thrown to indicate invalid credentials, but the producer remains open for the application to handle.
items.quote: The intention was to provide feedback via an exception if the producer was configured with invalid credentials. But we don't close the producer

items.rationale: Allows the application to retry authentication if credentials become available later.

items.rationale: The edge case where the selected fetch offset equals the leader's global log start offset causes an empty remote reconstruction range, leading to repeated retries and the replica being left out of the ISR.

A neighbour becomes coordinator and loads the partition from its own replica, which was never trimmed by a clean shutdown and never truncated by recovery, so the preallocated zero tail is still in the file. items.rationale: Highlights a critical limitation when using RESUME with production errors under EOS, which can lead to crash loops if the computation is deterministic.
items.title: EOS production errors may crash-loop
items.statement: Under EOS, returning RESUME for production errors may poison the transaction, causing the task to restart and reprocess the same bad record repeatedly.
items.quote: Under exactly-once semantics, a production error that triggers RESUME may poison the ongoing transaction. The task will restart from the last committed offset and reprocess the same input records. If the computation is deterministic, the same bad output record will be produced again, leading to a repeated cycle of failure → restart → failure.

items.rationale: Clarifies the behavior of RESUME for serialization errors, which is safe under both ALOS and EOS.
items.title: Serialization errors RESUME safely
items.statement: For serialization errors, RESUME works cleanly under both ALOS and EOS because the error occurs synchronously before the record reaches the producer.
items.quote: For serialization errors, this limitation does not apply — the error occurs synchronously before the record reaches the producer, so no transaction is affected and RESUME works cleanly under both ALOS and EOS.

items.rationale: Silent data loss during partition expansion is a correctness issue that users may not notice until it's too late.

items.statement: The current default reset policy ('latest') can silently lose data when partitions expand.

items.rationale: A safer default policy prevents data loss without requiring user awareness.

items.statement: Changing the default reset policy to 'by_duration:PT5S' protects users automatically from data loss.
items.quote: A safer default such as by_duration:PT5S protects users automatically, without requiring prior awareness of the issue.

items.rationale: Approach B is favored because it addresses a correctness issue sooner rather than later.
items.title: Default policy change approach
items.statement: The preferred approach is to change the default reset policy to 'by_duration:PT5S' in a 4.x minor release.
items.quote: I favor Approach B: Silent data loss during partition expansion is a correctness issue, not a usability issue.

items.rationale: A small replay window (5-10 seconds) is safer than silent data loss during partition expansion, as it covers the common metadata-blindness window while preserving the intent of the 'latest' policy for extended downtime.
items.title: Default reset policy changed to by_duration:PT5S
items.statement: The default auto.offset.reset and share.auto.offset.reset will be changed from 'latest' to 'by_duration:PT5S' to prevent silent data loss during partition expansion.
items.quote: by_duration:PT5S is already a valid value for both …

items.rationale: The project prioritizes consistency and simplicity in reset semantics, treating backlog uniformly regardless of partition age or consumer state.
items.title: Treat backlog uniformly
items.statement: Reset policies should not distinguish between historical data and live data; backlog should be treated uniformly.
items.quote: The central observation is that historical data and live data differ only in the amount of backlog involved.

items.title: Silent data loss risk with latest
items.statement: Using 'latest' as the reset policy can silently skip records produced to newly added partitions before the consumer becomes aware of them.
items.quote: When a topic is expanded, a consumer configured with auto.offset.reset=latest can silently miss every record produced to the newly added partitions before the consumer becomes aware of them.

items.rationale: The change must eliminate silent data loss for actively running consumers using the modern consumer group protocol during partition expansion.
items.title: Eliminate silent data loss for active consumers
items.statement: The change must prevent silent data loss during partition expansion for actively running consumers using the modern consumer group protocol.
items.quote: Eliminate silent data loss during partition expansion for the common case of actively running consumers using the modern consumer group protocol.

items.title: Bounded replay is safer than silent loss
items.statement: A bounded replay window (e.g., 5 seconds) is safer than silently skipping live data, as it ensures no data is permanently lost.
items.quote: The safer failure mode is bounded replay. With latest, records can be silently and permanently skipped. With by_duration:PT5S, the worst-case outcome is a bounded re-read of a few seconds of recent data.

items.rationale: PKCS error codes are often unhelpful for diagnosing TLS issues, making it harder for operators to debug.

items.quote: PKCS is notoriously cryptic with its error codes (with useful diagnostic messages such as “fatal_alert”, “PKIX invalid cert”/ “validation failed”)

items.rationale: Node replacement during KRaft migration breaks rollback capability if standard formatting is used.
items.title: Node replacement breaks KRaft rollback
items.statement: Replacing a node during KRaft migration using the standard kafka-storage.sh format command prevents rollback to ZooKeeper mode.
items.quote: when a broker is lost during the migration and the documented process for provisioning a replacement is followed, the replacement's storage is formatted using the kafka-storage.sh format procedure. That command unconditionally writes meta.properties with version=1. If a rollback is later required, the operator configures the brokers back into migration mode — at which point the newly provisioned broker rejects its own storage and crashes

items.rationale: The capability already exists in the broker and is cheap to expose, and removing the recovery path imposes unnecessary operational burden.
items.title: Add rollback-compatible storage format option
items.statement: A new optional flag (--zk-rollback-compatible) will be added to the kafka-storage.sh format command to enable rollback-compatible storage formatting.
items.quote: This KIP closes that gap.

items.rationale: Ensures the storage tool behaves consistently with the broker's migration mode formatting.
items.title: Storage tool must support version=0 meta.properties
items.statement: The storage tool must write meta.properties with version=0 when the --zk-rollback-compatible flag is used.
items.quote: When --zk-rollback-compatible is set, the storage tool selects MetaPropertiesVersion.V0 instead of the default MetaPropertiesVersion.V1

items.rationale: The flag is only relevant during the rollback-eligible phase of KRaft migration.
items.title: Use flag only during rollback-eligible migration
items.statement: Operators should use the --zk-rollback-compatible flag only while a KRaft migration can still be rolled back.
items.quote: the documentation makes clear that the flag is only relevant while a migration can still be rolled back, and should no longer be used once the migration has been finalized

items.title: Pause/resume bug causes duplicate task IDs
items.statement: The pauseTask and resumeTask methods can cause a task to appear in both pausedTasks and updatingTasks maps, leading to duplicate TaskIds in DefaultStateUpdater.tasks().
items.quote: pauseTask does pausedTasks.put(id) then updatingTasks.remove(id), and resumeTask does the reverse, so for a short window the task is in both maps and streamOfTasks() lists it twice.

items.rationale: The 5-minute timeout can lead to duplicate task removals and exceptions, and should be aligned with the rebalance timeout or treated fatally.

items.quote: If we are going to put a timeout there, it should match the rebalance timeout and we should treat it fatally, I think.

items.title: ReadOnlyTask lacks equals/hashCode
items.statement: ReadOnlyTask does not implement equals/hashCode, causing duplicate TaskIds in the Set returned by DefaultStateUpdater.tasks().
items.quote: ReadOnlyTask has no equals/hashCode, so the returned Set does not collapse the two wrappers.

items.rationale: To prevent hangs when the state updater thread exits, pending removal futures must be completed.
items.title: Complete removal futures on thread exit
items.statement: The state updater must complete its outstanding removal futures when the thread stops to avoid hangs.
items.quote: Make the state updater complete its outstanding removal futures when the thread stops.

items.title: Segment interval formula for window/session stores
items.statement: The default segment interval for window and session stores is computed as max(retentionPeriod / 2, 60_000ms).
items.quote: the segment interval for window and session stores is computed automatically as max(retentionPeriod / 2, 60_000ms)

items.rationale: Changing retention without changing segment interval should not require a state store restore.
items.title: Retention change without segment interval change
items.statement: Changing retention must not require a full state store restore if the segment interval remains unchanged.
items.quote: changing retention without changing segment interval does not require a state store restore

items.rationale: To avoid excessive RocksDB instances and performance degradation.
items.title: Minimum segment interval constraint
items.statement: The segment interval must be at least 60,000 milliseconds (1 minute).
items.quote: Must be at least 60,000 milliseconds (1 minute)

items.rationale: To prevent performance degradation from a single window spanning multiple segments.
items.title: Window store segment interval constraint
items.statement: For window stores, the segment interval must be greater than or equal to the window size.
items.quote: For window stores: must be greater than or equal to windowSize

items.title: Segment interval impact on performance
items.statement: Smaller segments can improve cache-hit ratios and reduce RocksDB compaction overhead for active data.
items.quote: A user who knows their access pattern could benefit from smaller segments (e.g., 1 hour), keeping the active segment compact while still retaining historical data across many smaller segments

items.rationale: Bytes-based control was initially adopted but later deemed less useful due to pruning behavior, where the slowest group's threshold controls the prune point, making bytes less effective than count for bounding retained log size.
items.title: Revert to count-based snapshot frequency
items.statement: The KIP will revert from bytes-based to count-based snapshot frequency due to pruning behavior making bytes less useful.
items.quote: I shall revise the KIP back to a count based approach and follow up here.

items.rationale: The pruning mechanism waits for the slowest group on a state partition to snapshot before deleting old records, making the slowest group's threshold the controlling factor for retained log size.
items.title: Pruning waits for slowest group
items.statement: Pruning waits for the slowest group on a state partition to snapshot, so its threshold controls the retained log size.
items.quote: pruning has to wait for the slowest group on the state partition to snapshot before it can delete old records.

items.rationale: Update records are of fairly constant size, making count-based thresholds nearly equivalent to bytes-based thresholds in practice.
items.title: Update records have constant size
items.statement: Update records are of fairly constant size, so count-based thresholds yield similar results to bytes-based thresholds.
items.quote: I think we had earlier calculations showed update records are a fairly constant size, so a count gives nearly the same result.

items.rationale: The KIP proposes to reject topic configurations where min.insync.replicas exceeds the replication factor at the API boundary to prevent silent misconfigurations.

items.statement: Topic creation and configuration changes must reject min.insync.replicas values exceeding the replication factor with INVALID_CONFIG.
items.quote: This KIP proposes to reject such configurations at the API boundary, where the mistake is made: topic creation and topic-level configuration changes.

items.rationale: KIP-966 established that the effective minimum ISR is clamped to min(min.insync.replicas, replication factor), making higher values ineffective.
items.title: Effective min ISR clamping
items.statement: The effective minimum ISR of a partition is clamped to min(min.insync.replicas, replication factor).
items.quote: the effective minimum ISR of a partition is defined as min(min.insync.replicas, replication factor), and both the controller and the broker silently clamp to that value

items.rationale: Existing topics with invalid configurations are grandfathered to avoid breaking changes, relying on the clamp for safety.
items.title: Grandfather existing invalid topics
items.statement: Existing topics with min.insync.replicas above their replication factor must remain unchanged and rely on the clamp.
items.quote: Existing topics are grandfathered. No existing topic is touched, invalidated, or mutated by this KIP.

items.rationale: A misconfiguration where min.insync.replicas exceeds replication factor can cause producer failures and disk fills due to retriable exceptions.
items.title: Misconfiguration causes producer failures
items.statement: Setting min.insync.replicas higher than replication factor can cause NotEnoughReplicasException and disk fills.

items.title: Bug 1 persists in shutdownStateUpdater
items.statement: Bug 1 occurs when an interrupted thread causes waitForFuture() to restore the interrupt flag and throw IllegalStateException, aborting shutdownStateUpdater().
items.quote: Bug 1 is still present. If the calling thread is interrupted while a removal future is incomplete, waitForFuture() restores the interrupt flag and throws IllegalStateException. This aborts shutdownStateUpdater() and skips the remaining TaskManager cleanup.

items.rationale: To ensure proper cleanup during shutdown, all tasks (local, pending futures, and queue tasks) must be accounted for.
items.title: Cleanup must account for all tasks

items.rationale: To ensure data safety, the offset boundaries must be validated during mirroring.
items.title: Offset boundary validation for data safety
items.statement: Mirroring must enforce offset boundaries using max(dest log start offset, min(dest LEO, source committed offset)) to prevent data loss or corruption.
items.quote: max(dest log start offset, min(dest LEO, source committed offset))

items.rationale: Mirrored records skip timestamp validation to preserve source timestamps, relying on source leader validation.
items.title: Timestamp validation skipped for mirrored records
items.statement: Mirrored records do not undergo timestamp validation on the destination cluster to preserve source timestamps.
items.quote: mirrored records skip timestamp validation like how a follower does right now. Timestamp validation is skipped for mirrored records to preserve source timestamps.

items.rationale: The mirror.support.unclean.leader.election config prevents destination ULE from electing stale replicas.
items.title: mirror.support.unclean.leader.election prevents destination ULE issues
items.statement: The mirror.support.unclean.leader.election configuration ensures truncation waits for all replicas to converge on the destination cluster, preventing unclean leader elections.
items.quote: Destination. The mirror.support.unclean.leader.election config controls truncation behavior on the destination cluster. This prevents a destination ULE from electing a replica that has stale pre-truncation data.
